decisions.reason: The give-up-year check is inside the calendar-exclusion loop, after advancing the candidate; it is not an unconditional upper-bound check on the initial candidate.

before.requirement: DoNothing asks for the next fire after current time, advances past calendar-excluded candidates, stops when no next time exists or the give-up year is exceeded, then sets NextFireTimeUtc.

after.requirement: DoNothing obtains a candidate using GetFireTimeAfter(current UTC time). While a candidate exists and a supplied calendar excludes it, it advances to the next candidate, exits if none exists, and clears a newly advanced candidate if its year exceeds YearToGiveUpSchedulingAt. It then assigns the resulting candidate or null to NextFireTimeUtc. With no calendar or an initially included candidate, the loop and its year check are skipped.

decisions.reason: The original startup exception is rethrown only if ShutdownSchedulers succeeds. Cleanup failures can replace it; the present unconditional wording hides a directly relevant startup-failure condition.

before.requirement: StartAsync catches OperationCanceledException without rethrow; other exceptions observed in its try cause ShutdownSchedulers with CancellationToken.None and rethrow. Do not imply this catch observes every later detached startup-task failure or prove runtime execution.

after.requirement: StartAsync swallows OperationCanceledException observed in its try. Other exceptions observed there cause an awaited ShutdownSchedulers(CancellationToken.None); the original exception is rethrown if cleanup succeeds, while a cleanup failure escapes instead. An incomplete deferred startup task is not awaited by StartAsync, so its later failures are not covered by this catch. These paths establish no observed execution.

decisions.reason: WhenAny completion does not await its winning task, propagate its exception, or cancel startup; the early return also prevents runtime-tenant draining through this StopCore invocation.

before.requirement: StopCore returns if its scheduler list is empty; otherwise waits for startupTask or cancellation delay and always calls ShutdownSchedulers in finally.

after.requirement: StopCore returns immediately if the hosted scheduler list is empty, without invoking ShutdownSchedulers or draining runtime tenants. Otherwise, if startupTask exists, it awaits Task.WhenAny(startupTask, an infinite delay using the stop token); it neither awaits the winning task nor cancels startup itself. Its finally invokes ShutdownSchedulers with the first stop caller's token even when that token is canceled.

decisions.reason: Attempt-all applies to the collected list after discovery succeeds. Runtime service resolution, TakeLiveSchedulers, or named options lookup precede the per-shutdown try blocks and can abort this path. Do not claim unconditional exhaustive shutdown.

before.requirement: All shutdown calls are initiated before awaiting their tasks, passing each WaitForJobsToComplete option and common cancellation token; synchronous throws become failed tasks.

after.requirement: Once scheduler discovery and named-options retrieval have completed successfully, ShutdownSchedulers initiates every collected scheduler's Shutdown call before awaiting the resulting tasks. It passes each scheduler's WaitForJobsToComplete and the common cancellation token; synchronous exceptions from invoking Shutdown or converting its ValueTask become failed tasks. A failure while collecting runtime schedulers/options occurs outside these per-scheduler catches and can prevent this loop.

decisions.reason: The prompt asks for change-impact analysis, not a requirement that every possible proposed change preserve current policy. Also bound aggregation to exceptions observed from the created shutdown tasks.

before.requirement: Each task is awaited with errors collected, then AggregateException is thrown if any failed. Changes must preserve that attempt-all policy; declarations alone prove no observed shutdown or completion.

after.requirement: Each created shutdown task is awaited with exceptions collected, and a nonempty collection produces AggregateException. A change to invocation or awaiting order can alter overlapping waits and the existing attempt-all/error-aggregation behavior. This is static behavior of the hosted-service path, not proof of shutdown or job completion; no assertion that arbitrary proposed changes must preserve this policy is required.

decisions.reason: FromContainer suppresses direct job disposal, but does not establish that every resolved object is owned by this scope. Singleton or externally supplied instances have different ownership. The implementation proves delegation to container lifetime rules, not unconditional scope ownership.

before.requirement: Scoped creation opens scope, calls ConfigureScope before ResolveJob, and records disposeJob=!fromContainer in ScopeState; container-resolved jobs are owned by the scope.

after.requirement: Scoped creation opens a scope, invokes ConfigureScope before ResolveJob, and records disposeJob = !fromContainer in ScopeState. Keyed or unkeyed container resolution sets fromContainer=true, so this factory does not directly dispose that job; it disposes the scope and leaves job ownership to container registration/lifetime rules. Factory activation sets fromContainer=false, so ScopeState attempts direct job disposal before disposing the scope.

decisions.reason: The original wording overgeneralizes creation failures and implies the original exception always survives scope disposal. CreateScope is outside the try; disposal can mask the original failure. The inherited property-application phase has a different cleanup policy and lies on the public creation path.

before.requirement: Creation failure disposes the newly created scope before rethrowing through ExceptionDispatchInfo; normal ReturnJob cannot be relied on for this failed creation path.

after.requirement: If ConfigureScope or ResolveJob fails after the scope was opened, CreateJobInstance attempts scope disposal itself; if disposal succeeds it rethrows the original failure via ExceptionDispatchInfo, but a disposal failure replaces it. CreateScope itself is outside this try. A failure before JobScope is returned cannot rely on normal ReturnJob. Separately, the inherited CreateJob calls ReturnJob when ApplyProperties fails after a JobScope exists; it logs cleanup failure and preserves that property-application exception.

decisions.reason: Disposal is conditional on disposable interfaces; the shared sentinel does not supply a per-job duplicate-disposal guard. Constructor failure is also relevant to the requested unscoped failure path.

before.requirement: Unscoped construction returns Unscoped sentinel state; ReturnJob disposes its job directly.

after.requirement: Successful unscoped construction returns the Unscoped sentinel state. Constructor exceptions become a faulted ValueTask<JobScope>. ReturnJob recognizing this sentinel calls DisposeIfDisposable on the job: async disposal is preferred, otherwise synchronous disposal is used, and nondisposable jobs are left alone. This branch has no ScopeState-style duplicate-disposal guard.

decisions.reason: Replacement state is disposed only when disposable; the actual helper must be cited, not just the XML documentation asserting that condition.

before.requirement: ReturnJob delegates ScopeState disposal to that state, but for replacement state it disposes the replacement and leaves the job alone; derived factories own cascading cleanup or must override ReturnJob.

after.requirement: ReturnJob delegates its own ScopeState to DisposeAsync. For state that is neither ScopeState nor the Unscoped sentinel, it leaves the job untouched and calls DisposeIfDisposable on the replacement state, preferring async disposal and doing nothing for nondisposable state. A derived factory must preserve/cascade original cleanup through its replacement state or override ReturnJob to perform that teardown.

decisions.reason: The guard permits one disposal attempt, not guaranteed successful disposal or shared completion for concurrent callers. Scope cleanup is attempted even if job cleanup fails; a finally exception can mask the job-disposal exception.

before.requirement: ScopeState uses Interlocked.Exchange to permit disposal once; disposes only factory-activated jobs and disposes the scope in finally. DisposeScope prefers IAsyncDisposable, falling back to synchronous Dispose.

after.requirement: ScopeState uses Interlocked.Exchange(ref disposed, 1) before cleanup so only the first caller attempts disposal; later callers return immediately, do not join that attempt, and cannot retry a failed attempt. Only factory-activated jobs are passed to DisposeIfDisposable. The scope is disposed in finally, preferring IAsyncDisposable and otherwise IDisposable; this is an attempt, not a guarantee of successful cleanup. A scope-disposal exception can replace a job-disposal exception.

scoring_decision: Accept explicit partial-credit and normative-claim rules; clarify strict scoring per task and corpus. Prompts unchanged.
